overview.text: Octane rating, also called octane number, describes how well a spark-ignition fuel resists auto-ignition as it is compressed. If fuel-air mixture ignites too early, it can cause engine knock, a pinging combustion event that may damage an engine. The rating compares a fuel’s knock behavior with reference fuels: iso-octane is assigned 100 and n-heptane 0. Standardized engine tests measure this resistance. In the United States, pump labels commonly show the average of research and motor octane numbers, which are measured under different operating conditions. A higher number indicates greater knock resistance, but does not mean every engine needs the highest grade.

key_facts.text: Knock occurs when unburned fuel-air mixture auto-ignites under high temperature and pressure before the advancing flame reaches it.
The reference value 100 is assigned to iso-octane (2,2,4-trimethylpentane); n-heptane is assigned 0.
In the United States, the pump label’s (R+M)/2 value is the average of research octane number (RON) and motor octane number (MON).
RON and MON tests use different operating conditions; MON testing uses higher air temperature and engine speed than RON testing.
An international standard describes determining MON with a standardized, variable-compression test engine.
